client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just can't seem to enjoy it the way I used to — her absence feels so loud, if that makes any sense. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: What you're describing makes complete sense — grief has a way of making someone's absence feel almost tangible, especially in the spaces where they used to be most present. It takes real courage to show up here even when you're not sure it will help, and that willingness itself matters. I'm wondering, when you're at those family gatherings and her absence feels so loud, what does that moment usually feel like for you on the inside?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It's like this hollow, heavy feeling in my chest — almost like I'm waiting for her to walk through the door or say something, and then I remember she won't. I end up kind of zoning out from whatever conversation is happening around me, and I feel guilty about that, like I'm failing the rest of my family by not being more present. It's a weird mix of sadness and this anxious pressure to just act normal so I don't bring everyone else down.
therapist: That guilt you're describing — feeling like you're "failing" your family by grieving — is such a common but painful trap, and it's worth gently questioning whether that's really true or whether it's your mind adding an extra burden on top of an already heavy loss. You're not zoning out because you don't care about them; you're zoning out because you're carrying something enormous. I'm curious, do you think the rest of your family might actually be feeling something similar, just maybe expressing it differently?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Maybe, but honestly my family isn't really the type to talk about feelings openly, so it's hard to know what anyone else is actually going through. My aunt seemed fine at the last gathering, laughing and telling stories, and part of me almost resented that — like, how can she just move on like that? I know that's probably not fair of me, but it made me feel even more alone in what I was feeling.
therapist: That feeling of resentment makes a lot of sense — when we're in pain and someone else seems untouched by it, it can feel isolating and even a little unfair, even if we know logically that people grieve differently. Your aunt's laughter might actually be *her* way of carrying the same loss, just in a language your family has learned to speak instead of silence. I'm wondering, in a family where feelings don't get talked about openly, where have *you* typically taken your grief when it needed somewhere to go?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, mostly nowhere — I just kind of sit with it by myself, late at night when everything is quiet. I'll look at old photos on my phone or reread texts she sent me, which I know probably isn't helping me move forward, but it feels like the only way I can still be close to her. I don't really have anyone I feel comfortable enough to talk to about this, which is part of why being here feels so strange and unfamiliar.
therapist: Those quiet late-night moments with her photos and texts aren't a sign that you're doing grief "wrong" — they're actually a testament to how much she meant to you, and that connection is real and worth honoring. And the fact that being here feels strange makes complete sense when you've been carrying this so privately for so long. I'm glad you took that unfamiliar step anyway — what is it like, even just right now, to say some of this out loud to someone else for the first time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: It's actually a little bit of a relief, which surprises me because I expected to just feel exposed or embarrassed. But there's also this nagging voice in the back of my head saying that talking about it doesn't actually bring her back or fix anything, so what's the point. I guess I'm not sure how to trust that this process is going somewhere useful when the loss itself isn't going to change.
therapist: That relief you felt is actually really meaningful data about you — part of you clearly needed this more than you expected, even if another part is still skeptical. The "what's the point" voice is understandable, because you're right that talking can't undo the loss, but what therapy can do is help you carry it differently so it doesn't have to be so isolating and heavy. I'm curious about that nagging voice — does it show up in other areas of your life too, or does it feel specific to grief?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That voice is pretty familiar, honestly — it shows up a lot, like when I try something new and immediately start questioning whether it's worth the effort before I've even given it a chance. I think it's tied to this fear of being disappointed, like if I don't expect much then I can't really be let down. With the grief though it feels sharper, maybe because my grandmother was one of the few people who made me feel like I wasn't alone, and losing her kind of took that safety net away.
therapist: What you just shared feels really significant — that your grandmother wasn't just someone you loved, but someone who made you feel fundamentally less alone in the world, and that her loss has left a particular kind of vulnerability that goes beyond ordinary grief. That pattern of bracing for disappointment before it can find you makes so much sense as a way of protecting yourself, especially now that one of your safest relationships is gone. I'm wondering, when you imagine what it might feel like to let this process matter to you — to actually let yourself hope it helps — what comes up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, imagining that feels kind of scary — like if I let myself hope this helps and then it doesn't, I'll just end up feeling more alone than before. It's almost easier to keep that wall up, even though I can hear how that sounds. I guess I'm just not sure I know how to let something matter without it also becoming something that could hurt me.
therapist: What you just described is one of the most human dilemmas there is — that the things most worth having are also the things that can hurt us most, and your heart seems to understand that very clearly right now. That wall you're describing isn't a flaw; it's something you built for good reasons, and it's kept you safe, but it sounds like part of you is also aware of what it costs you. I'm curious — when you said "I can hear how that sounds," what did you imagine I might be thinking about you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think I assumed you'd see me as someone who's being self-defeating, like I'm standing in my own way and should just know better. There's this part of me that worries I come across as too guarded or difficult to help, which I guess is kind of ironic given what we're talking about. It's strange to even say that out loud because I realize I'm doing the same thing here — bracing for judgment before you've actually given me any reason to expect it.
therapist: The fact that you caught yourself doing it in real time — bracing for my judgment before I'd given you any reason to — is actually a really important moment of self-awareness, and it's the opposite of self-defeating. What I actually notice is someone who is thoughtful, honest, and trying hard even while feeling scared, which takes more courage than people who find this easy. I'm also noticing you seem to be carrying a lot right now as you say this — would it feel okay to just slow down a little and let this moment of insight settle rather than rushing past it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I'm sitting with that and it feels uncomfortable in a way that's hard to explain — like receiving a compliment when you're used to bracing for criticism, and not quite knowing what to do with it. Part of me wants to deflect or say "well, you're just saying that," but I'm trying to notice that impulse instead of just acting on it. I think slowing down is harder than it sounds for me, because when things get quiet I usually just end up back inside my own head where it's not very kind.
therapist: The way you just caught that impulse to deflect and chose to name it instead — that *is* slowing down, even if it doesn't feel like it yet. And what you said about your own head not being a kind place when things get quiet is something I really want us to return to, because it sounds like you've been living with a pretty harsh inner voice for a long time. I'm wondering, if your grandmother were here and could hear the way you talk to yourself on the inside, what do you think she would say?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: She would probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself — she had this way of saying it that didn't feel like a dismissal, it actually felt like she meant it and could see something in me I couldn't see in myself. Just thinking about that makes my throat tighten, because that voice is gone now and I don't really have anything to replace it with. I guess that's part of what makes the silence so hard — it used to have her in it.
therapist: What you just described is such a tender and important thing — she didn't just love you, she *saw* you, and that kind of being-seen is irreplaceable in a way that ordinary grief doesn't quite capture. I notice as you said that, your voice became very soft, like you were holding something fragile, and I just want to make space for that without rushing past it. That voice she carried about you — the one that saw something you couldn't see in yourself — I wonder if any part of it has stayed with you, even now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
